content.text: are the optimizer's predictions in its own units, not measured time, and an actual plan still shows the same predicted costs. They're wrong whenever an estimate is wrong or some work isn't costed at all. To find where a query spends its time, read the actual numbers: rows against estimates, executions, elapsed and CPU time per operator, and reads.

A report query takes about 3 seconds. Its plan has two operators: a Clustered Index Scan at 95% of the cost and a Compute Scalar at 5%. So the team adds a covering index to get rid of the scan. In a test on SQL Server 2022, that index cut the plan's estimated cost from 10.4 to 0.14, and the query took 3.2 seconds. The 5% operator was calling a scalar function, and more than 90% of the elapsed time was spent inside it.
The belief: the percentage on each operator shows how much of the query's time that operator takes, so you fix the biggest one.

It's an easy belief to hold. The number is labelled "cost", it's the most visible number on the plan, and SQL Server Management Studio prints it on every operator of an actual plan too, which looks like a measurement. When every estimate is accurate and every step is costed, cost often does track the real work, so the habit gets rewarded often enough to stick.
Cost is a prediction, in the optimizer's own units

Both engines choose plans by estimated cost. Microsoft describes SQL Server's optimizer as cost-based: each candidate plan has a cost in computing resources, the optimizer picks one with a low estimated cost, and it relies on statistics to estimate it. PostgreSQL's docs are blunt about the units: costs are arbitrary, traditionally in units of disk page fetches, while

reports actual time in milliseconds, "so they are unlikely to match up". The cost also leaves things out; PostgreSQL's, for example, ignores the time to send rows to the client. A percentage is just one operator's share of that predicted total.
An actual plan doesn't replace the estimates
An actual plan adds runtime information to the compiled plan; it doesn't recompute the costs. In the plan XML from the test, each operator carried its

and, separately, measured counters: actual rows, executions, elapsed and CPU milliseconds, logical reads. The percentages come from the first set. The scan was 95% of the estimated cost; measured, it took between 80 and 210 ms of a query that ran 2.7 to 4.7 seconds across seven runs.
Some work isn't costed at all

Microsoft's page on scalar UDF inlining lists "lack of costing" among the reasons scalar functions perform poorly: the optimizer costs relational operators but not scalar ones, so an expensive function call can still look nearly free. In the test, the function ran a query per row, 35,202 times. Its queries don't appear in the outer plan, and
listed only the 11,972 reads of the outer scan. The root operator's
Every cost is built on a

: how many rows the optimizer expects at each step. If it expects 1 row and gets 100,000, every cost on that branch was computed for the wrong amount of work, and so was every percentage. PostgreSQL's docs name the first thing to check: whether the estimated row counts are reasonably close to reality. A later article in this path covers where those estimates come from.

rows.text: Share of the optimizer's estimated total, in its own units
Measured; in PostgreSQL, rows and time are per-loop averages
Spot bad estimates and repeated work
Compare the I/O of two versions

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
✅ Right
tabs.code:
-- The same result as a set-based query the optimizer can see and cost
SELECT o.Id, o.Total,
       CASE WHEN t.Total > 5000 THEN 'Gold' ELSE 'Standard' END AS Tier
FROM dbo.Orders AS o
CROSS APPLY (SELECT SUM(x.Total) AS Total
             FROM dbo.Orders AS x
             WHERE x.CustomerId = o.CustomerId) AS t
WHERE o.CreatedAt >= '2025-11-01';
-- Estimated cost 12.5, higher than the UDF version. Tested: 0.13-0.15 s

content.text: The rewrite returned the same rows and ran about 20 times faster. Yet put both queries in one batch and their estimated costs, 10.4 and 12.5, make the rewrite 55% of the batch, as if it were the slower one. Comparing versions by "query cost relative to the batch" would have kept the 3-second query.
keeps the demo honest: SQL Server 2019 and later can inline many scalar functions, but not all of them.
To get the measured numbers, ask for them explicitly:

tabs.label: SQL Server
tabs.code:
SET STATISTICS XML ON;      -- actual plan with runtime counters
SET STATISTICS IO, TIME ON; -- reads per table, CPU and elapsed time
SELECT o.Id, o.Total, dbo.CustomerTier(o.CustomerId) AS Tier
FROM dbo.Orders AS o
WHERE o.CreatedAt >= '2025-11-01';

tabs.label: PostgreSQL
tabs.code:
-- ANALYZE runs the query; in PostgreSQL 18 it includes BUFFERS
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE)
SELECT id, total
FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= '2025-11-01';

How to apply it in your project

Read the total elapsed and CPU time first. In SQL Server, check

items.title: Walk the operators by measured time and rows

content.text: Look for the operators with the largest actual time and reads, and for estimated rows far from actual rows. Those gaps explain most bad plan choices.
Judge a rewrite or an index by elapsed time and reads over several runs, never by its cost percentage or its share of the batch.

items.text: Cost percentages are predicted shares in the optimizer's own units, and an actual plan still shows the predicted ones.
Work the optimizer doesn't cost, like a non-inlined scalar UDF, can take 95% of the time behind a 5% operator.
Every cost rests on row estimates; compare estimated rows with actual rows before trusting any percentage.
Find the time in actual elapsed and CPU time, executions or loops, and reads.
Compare query versions by measured time and reads: in the test, the faster rewrite had the higher estimated cost.
